meta.title: Who really said "What brings no benefit to the hive, brings none to the bee"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 6.54) — but this exact English wording is Robin Hard's 1997 translation, still in copyright. The free-to-reuse rendering is George Long's 1862. Cited by Spain coach Luis de la Fuente at the 2026 World Cup.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What brings no benefit to the hive, brings none to the bee'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes — it's Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 6.54). The exact wording is Robin Hard's 1997 translation; the public-domain version is George Long's 1862 'That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 121–180 AD · Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher
answer.sourceLine: The thought is authentically his — it is Meditations 6.54, a single sentence written in Greek. The exact English shown is Robin Hard’s 1997 translation (Oxford World’s Classics); the recognizable public-domain rendering is George Long’s 1862 “That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.”

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: What brings no benefit to the hive brings none to the bee.
trail: The exact popular wording — ‘What brings no benefit to the hive, brings none to the bee’ — is Robin Hard’s 1997 translation (Oxford World’s Classics), reproduced verbatim in the press translation comparison ↗.
The classic public-domain rendering is George Long’s 1862: ‘That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee’ Long’s full text ↗.

It surged in mid-July 2026 when Spain’s coach Luis de la Fuente cited it during the World Cup — ‘Lo que es malo para el panal es malo para la abeja’ — as a team-over-individual motto de la Fuente on Marcus Aurelius ↗.
source.excerptNote: Robin Hard’s 1997 rendering of Meditations 6.54 — the entire chapter is this one sentence. Long’s 1862 public-domain version reads ‘That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.’
source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek Meditations is long in the public domain, but the exact English wording shown — ‘What brings no benefit to the hive, brings none to the bee’ — is Robin Hard’s 1997 translation, which remains in copyright. Quoting it once with credit is fine; to reproduce the line freely, use a public-domain rendering such as George Long’s 1862 ‘That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.’

author.metaLine: 121–180 AD · Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher
author.bio: Marcus Aurelius (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors. His private notebook, known as the Meditations, was written in Greek during his military campaigns and never intended for publication. It survives as one of the most enduring works of Stoic philosophy, prized for its unguarded, practical reflections on self-discipline and the shaping of the mind.

misattribution.heading: Correct author, modern (copyrighted) wording
misattribution.intro: The saying is correctly Marcus Aurelius — the catch is the wording and its rights, not the authorship. He wrote a single Greek sentence; the polished English line in circulation is a specific modern translator’s work, still under copyright.

items.why: The exact English — ‘What brings no benefit to the hive, brings none to the bee’ — is Robin Hard’s 1997 Oxford translation, circulated with no translator credit. For free reuse, use George Long’s public-domain 1862 wording instead translations compared ↗.

Spain’s coach and the press render it ‘lo que es malo para el panal es malo para la abeja’ (‘what is bad for the hive is bad for the bee’) — the same 6.54, phrased in the negative rather than Hard’s ‘no benefit’ de la Fuente’s quote ↗.

Standard versions differ: George Long (1862) ‘not good for the swarm’; Gregory Hays (2003) ‘What injures the hive injures the bee.’ Only Hard gives the familiar ‘no benefit to the hive’ line Wikiquote/WIST ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 6.54) — but the exact English is Robin Hard’s 1997 translation (in copyright); George Long’s 1862 ‘not good for the swarm’ is the free-to-reuse rendering ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Stoicism holds that a person is part of a larger whole — a limb of a body, a bee in a hive. Marcus Aurelius’ one-line chapter 6.54 draws the practical conclusion: your interests and the community’s are not opposed, so what damages the group damages you too.

It surfaced in mid-July 2026 when Spain’s national-team coach Luis de la Fuente, an open admirer of the Meditations, quoted it to explain putting the team above any individual — ‘what is bad for the hive is bad for the bee.’
detailsBody: George Long (1862): ‘That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.’
Haines / Loeb (1916): ‘That which is not in the interests of the hive cannot be in the interests of the bee.’
Robin Hard (1997): ‘What brings no benefit to the hive brings none to the bee.’
Gregory Hays (2003): ‘What injures the hive injures the bee.’
